AI Agent 学习与求职整理文档

适合研一阶段建立能力栈、做项目与准备实习投递

这份文档聚焦 AI Agent 方向：解释岗位本质、总结核心技能栈、给出学习优先级，并附上项目建议、简历要点与 12 周执行路线。
目标不是“学很多概念”，而是尽快形成可展示的工程能力与作品集。



1. AI Agent 到底是什么

AI Agent 岗位通常不是单纯“训练一个大模型”，而是围绕大模型构建一个能完成复杂任务的系统。它会综合使用提示词、检索、工具调用、工作流编排、状态管理、评测与监控，让模型能够在真实业务场景中稳定工作。

因此，对实习生最重要的能力不是只会调用 API，而是能够把模型能力组织成一个可调试、可评估、可部署的应用。

2. 岗位能力拆解

可以把 AI Agent 方向拆成四层能力：

模型理解层：知道 LLM 的能力边界、上下文窗口、结构化输出、工具调用、推理链路与常见失败模式。

应用架构层：会搭建 RAG、单 Agent、多 Agent 或 Workflow 系统，能设计任务拆分与状态流转。

工程落地层：会用 FastAPI、数据库、向量库、缓存、日志、Docker 等把系统部署起来。

评测与优化层：能衡量回答质量、检索效果、工具调用成功率、时延与成本，并据此做迭代。

3. 研一阶段最该优先学习的内容

3.1 编程与工程基础

Python：熟练掌握函数、类、装饰器、异常处理、文件读写、异步、虚拟环境。

Linux 与 Git：命令行操作、SSH、进程、日志、Git 分支与协作。

后端基础：FastAPI 或 Flask，理解接口设计、请求响应、鉴权与错误处理。

数据库与缓存：至少了解 PostgreSQL/MySQL、Redis 的基础使用场景。

Docker：会把一个 Agent 项目封装成可运行服务。

3.2 模型与算法基础

机器学习基础：监督学习、损失函数、过拟合、泛化、评估指标。

深度学习基础：反向传播、优化器、Transformer 的核心机制。

NLP/LLM 基础：Token、Embedding、Attention、Prompt、上下文长度、采样参数。

3.3 Agent 核心知识

Prompt 设计：角色设定、任务约束、输出格式、few-shot 示例。

Structured Output：让模型输出 JSON 或明确字段，方便下游程序消费。

Tool Calling：让模型选择并调用外部工具，例如搜索、数据库查询、代码执行。

RAG：文档切分、向量化、检索、重排、引用来源。

Memory：会话记忆、用户偏好存储、长期记忆与状态管理。

Workflow vs Agent：知道什么时候用固定流程，什么时候让模型自主决策。

Eval：构建测试集，衡量准确率、召回率、拒答质量与工具成功率。

5. 最值得做的项目

项目一：带引用的 RAG 问答系统

输入一组 PDF 或网页文档，实现切分、索引、检索、重排与引用展示。

支持多轮追问，避免幻觉，并能说明答案来自哪里。

这是最基础也最能体现工程能力的项目。

项目二：工具调用型 Agent

例如做一个“日程助手”“邮件助手”或“SQL 数据分析助手”。

重点展示模型如何判断是否需要调用工具、如何处理异常、如何返回结构化结果。

这个项目体现你对 tool calling 和系统边界的理解。

项目三：多 Agent / Workflow 项目

例如“研究员 Agent + 写作 Agent + 审核 Agent”的报告生成系统。

重点是状态流转清晰、职责划分明确，并能说明为什么要多 Agent 而不是一个大 prompt。

这个项目可以作为简历上的高级项。

6. 学习顺序与避坑建议

先补 Python、Linux、Git、FastAPI、Docker，不要一开始就沉迷各种框架名词。

先做单 Agent 或固定 Workflow，再做多 Agent；很多初学者过早追求“复杂架构”。

先把 RAG 做扎实，再谈“自主规划”；检索和评测往往比 fancy prompt 更重要。

不要只会调接口，要学会日志、错误重试、成本控制和性能分析。

每做完一个项目，都准备 README、架构图、演示视频和可复现步骤。

7. 简历与面试中最该强调什么

Abstract— In robot scientific laboratories, visual anomaly de-
tection is important for the timely identification and resolution

ensuring the stability and safety of experimental processes. To

first-person visual observation can effectively identify process-
level anomalies. This work provides both a data-driven founda-
tion and an evaluation framework for vision anomaly detection
in scientific experiment workflows.

multimodal reasoning capabilities, supporting zero-shot
anomaly detection via context-aware VQA [13], [16], pre-

decision-making in experimental workflows. Specifically, we
propose a method that utilizes visual information collected
during experimental execution, combined with structured

VLMs. As shown in Fig.2, this approach integrates experi-

A complete automated experimental workflow, as illus-
trated in Fig.2, can be formally represented by an ordered
set of steps S = {s1,s2, . . . ,sn} along with fundamental infor-
mation I about the context of the experiment. Each step si,
defined as a meta-step, may include one or multiple robotic
actions. Each meta-step si requires certain prerequisites (e.g.,
materials, reagents, or equipment) and completion condi-
tions, which together serve as the anomaly detection target
C, and may include a fine-grained anomaly description Cd.
To support different levels of prompt granularity in anomaly
detection, we introduce an information control function
φ (S,C,Cd), which determines the semantic content provided
to the model during inference. Given a visual observation x
captured from the experiment, the anomaly detection task is
formulated as a binary classification function:
judgeAnomaly(x,I, φ (S,C,Cd)) → y (1)
where y ∈ {0,1} indicates whether an anomaly is present
(1 for anomaly, 0 for normal). The function φ selectively
includes the step information S, the detection target C, and
the fine-grained anomaly description Cd, depending on the
evaluation configuration. Formally, φ serves as a semantic
controller that determines the composition and granularity
of the prompt content. One specific instantiation of φ is pre-
sented in Section IV to support hierarchical prompt analysis.
This formulation provides a unified framework for mod-
eling open-ended reasoning and goal-conditioned anomaly
detection, and serves as the foundation for our benchmark’s
layered evaluation strategy.

A. Experimental Setup
We evaluate two representative VLMs: GPT-4o and
Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct. The latter is abbreviated as
QwenVL-72B. Both models are capable of performing
image-text reasoning and support natural language prompt-
ing. Inference is conducted via publicly available APIs,
without any fine-tuning.
In addition, we perform a real-world validation in a robotic
laboratory, where anomaly detection is performed through a
GPT-4o-driven reasoning pipeline to verify model behavior
in actual experimental procedures.
B. Evaluation Metrics
To comprehensively evaluate model performance, we
adopt the following four metrics:
Accuracy (ACC) : The percentage of samples correctly
classified as normal or abnormal, indicating the overall
effectiveness.
False Positive Rate (FPR) : The percentage of normal
samples incorrectly predicted as abnormal. This reflects the
model’s tendency to generate false alarms, which may cause
unnecessary workflow interruptions.
Missed Detection Rate (MDR): The percentage of abnor-
mal samples mistakenly classified as normal, representing the
model’s failure to detect true anomalies - a critical factor in
high-risk experimental contexts.
Uncertainty Rate (UR) : The percentage of cases where
the model cannot provide a confident judgment. This metric
indicates the model’s ambiguity when handling visually
complex or previously unseen samples, and provides insight
into its robustness and reliability.

D. Real-World Demonstration
To further validate the benchmark’s applicability, we con-
ducted a real-world test in a robotic chemical laboratory. The
test focused on the operation where a robotic arm transfers a
silicone bottle from the material table to the operation table.
As shown in Fig.6, the experiment is divided into two key
checkpoints: before and after the execution of the transfer
step. At the beginning of the step, the model receives the
experiment background and step description as input, and
is prompted to check whether the silicone bottle is present
on the material table. The model correctly responds with no
anomaly, confirming that the setup is valid.
After the robotic arm completes the transfer, another image
is captured at the workbench. The model is again prompted
to verify whether the silicone bottle has been successfully
placed. The result is also no anomaly, demonstrating the
model’s ability to monitor the correctness of step execution
under real-world conditions.
